OEBPS/xhtml/03_Fm01.xhtml:
FOREIGN MILITARY STUDIES

History is replete with examples of notable military campaigns and exceptional military leaders and theorists. Military professionals and students of the art and science of war cannot afford to ignore these sources of knowledge or limit their studies to the history of the U.S. armed forces. This series features original works, translations, and reprints of classics outside the American canon that promote a deeper understanding of international military theory and practice.

The Institute for Advanced Military Thinking (IAMT) was formed by retired senior officers of the Israel Defense Forces to serve as a bridge between the theories and policies of the academic world and the doctrine, training, and other preparations required for field operations. The IAMT applies this approach across the full spectrum of future land warfare by:

•  initiating and supporting joint discussions regarding the historical lessons offered by land warfare in the Middle East;

•  encouraging innovative thinking and open debate about current critical defense issues;

•  supporting decision makers as they prepare for future challenges.

SERIES EDITORS: Roger Cirillo and Gideon Avidor

An AUSA Book

OEBPS/xhtml/08_Foreword.xhtml:
Foreword

In this book, Pesach Malovany has created a fascinating mosaic of the Iraqi Army and of a world that once was, but has ceased to exist. By doing so he affords sharp, profound insights into the factors that led to the disintegration of that world. This was the world of the Iraqi regime under the leadership of the dictator Saddam Hussein, which may be seen clearly through the prism of the army, its structure, internal balance of power, and position in Iraqi society. The text makes an important contribution to understanding these processes in the past, the present, and the possible future.

By depicting the Iraqi Army and the broader picture reflected by it through painstaking, exhaustive research, Pesach Malovany has created a masterwork that yet again demonstrates that the intelligence officer, apparently a passive bystander, must possess patience, discernment, diagnostic ability, sophisticated information-gathering techniques, and analytical skill. All these elements might be attainable by others, but not everyone has the ability to fit all the pieces of the puzzle into a fascinating, significant whole that contributes greatly to comprehending the reality of the world as it is.

Wars of Modern Babylon is the first document of its kind, drawing a portrait of an Arab army from its own point of view, as it chooses to present itself. Such a text has even more importance and validity when it focuses on the army of a country that has made a superhuman effort to arm itself with unconventional weaponry, including long-range missiles that have on occasion been directed at the State of Israel, turning it into an imminent regional threat.

Colonel (Ret.) Pesach Malovany is a senior intelligence analyst who served for many years in the collection and research units of the Intelligence Corps, the fruits of whose labors I enjoyed in my capacity as a former Director of Military Intelligence.

Lt. Gen. (Ret.) Amnon Lipkin-Shahak
Former Director of Military Intelligence
and Chief of the General Staff, Israel Defense Forces 2010
OEBPS/xhtml/09_Foreword.xhtml:
Foreword

After having disappeared from the world as a result of the Second Gulf War, the Iraqi Army has been bestowed a worthy memorial. Colonel (Ret.) Pesach Malovany, a veteran researcher of Iraq in general, and of its army in particular, has painstakingly collected every scrap of information that it has been possible to obtain regarding this huge army, which for many years was the driving force behind the “Eastern Front” threatening Israel’s security.

The Iraqi Army played an important role in two of Israel’s wars (although, despite its efforts, not in the Six-Day War):

A.  The War of Independence: As part of the Eastern Front that (as uncoordinated as it was) included the armies of Transjordan, Iraq, and Syria, which attacked along the entire length of the border between the Dead Sea and the Upper Galilee. The Iraqi Army initially attacked in the center (the Jordan Valley area) in the direction of Kochav Hayarden, and toward the town of Afula. After the initial phase of the fighting (which did not yield any real results), the Iraqi forces were transferred to the area of Qalqilya-Jenin, and were responsible in no small part for the fact that the waist of the State of Israel remained very narrow in the vicinity of Kfar Yona, as well as the failure of the IDF to conquer the Jenin area. The Iraqi Army retreated at the war’s end, but Iraq, unlike the immediate neighbors of the newly created State of Israel, never signed a ceasefire agreement with Israel, and the state of war between the two nations never formally ended.

B.  The Yom Kippur War: Twenty-five years later, the Iraqi Army came to the aid of the Syrian Army, which was withstanding with difficulty an IDF counterattack on the Golan Heights. It is possible that without that aid, which surprised the IDF at its major breakthrough point (the Laner Division sector) when the Syrian Army was in retreat under the pressure of Israeli attack, the war would have ended with a much greater Syrian defeat, and the IDF might have succeeded in totally decimating the Syrian forces and reaching the outskirts of Damascus.

From that time on, the Iraqi Army has been considered a force that could overturn the balance of power between Israel and her neighbors, making an eastern front a powerful threat to Israel’s ability to defend herself. The possible recruitment of this huge army turned every scenario of an attack from the east into a nightmare for Israel military strategists.

This threat was removed when the United States Army took control of Iraq; however, becoming acquainted with this army that disappeared from the face of the earth demonstrates the military potential inherent in a huge country lying to the east of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. Since geography is unchanging, and Iraq is liable in the future to become a more relevant threat than it is today, it is worthwhile becoming familiar with the military power that it once was, even if the army described in this book belongs to history and no longer exists (although its remnants form the hard core of Sunni resistance to the New Iraq).

The Iraqi Army is an interesting phenomenon as a professional army that preserved the characteristics of British influence for many years after the British had evacuated the region altogether and had been driven out of Iraq in disgrace. This influence remained even after, for political reasons, the Soviet Union became Iraq’s major arms supplier, and Iraqi officers began receiving their training in Moscow.

Never before has such a detailed book been written about an Arab army, and we must be grateful to Col. Pesach Malovany, who took this on as a personal project over an extended period of time. I have no doubt that anyone wishing to become familiar with and understand the history of the Middle East (from its reconstruction after the fall of the Ottoman Empire in the First World War until the conquest of Iraq by the United States as a result of the Second Gulf War [2003]) will be greatly enlightened by this book. This stems from the simple fact that what occurred in the area in the course of those 80 years is difficult to comprehend without taking Iraq and its military power into account.

This book is a monument to an army that is no more and a regime that has disappeared from the face of the earth. It may be assumed that in the future any army constructed in Iraq will not resemble the one dating back to the Ba’ath period, and in this lies the importance of studying Iraq’s military history prior to 2003 (the U.S. occupation) and its influence on the entire region.

Maj. Gen. (Ret.) Ya’akov Amidror
Former National Security Advisor, Israel 2010
OEBPS/xhtml/10_Preface.xhtml:
Preface and Acknowledgments

This book describes and analyzes the development and activities of the Iraqi Army from its establishment in 1921 until its collapse in 2003 as a result of the war against the Coalition forces, the core of which was a highly intensive 24-year period under the leadership of Saddam Hussein.

The book focuses on the major wars in which the Iraqi Army participated during Saddam’s regime. These included the prolonged war against Iran (1980–1988) and the two wars against the Coalition forces led by the United States (1991 and 2003). In addition, processes of acquisition of armaments and strengthening of both conventional and unconventional capabilities are depicted, as well as the wars against Israel and the Kurds in which Iraq participated during earlier periods.

The major innovation of this book lies in its presenting this topic to the reader—including all the elements of the construction of the Iraqi fighting force, its war strategies, its functioning on all levels (strategic, operative and tactical), its forces and branches—in a comprehensive, detailed manner, and all of this chiefly from an Iraqi point of view.

The chief source on which the book is based is the Iraqi press during the Saddam era (1979–2003), which over the years published a rich corpus of information on military matters, including interviews with and memoirs of officers at various levels, in addition to articles involving the political leadership and Saddam at its head. The sources include the daily newspapers Al-Thawrah, Al-Jumhuriyah, Al-Iraq, Al-Qadisiyah, and Babel (Babil), the weekly Alif Baa, and the monthly Huras al-Watan. Additional invaluable sources were books written by key figures in the Iraqi regime, the army high command, and local analysts. Some of these were published under the auspices of the Iraqi government, while others were written by individuals who escaped from Iraq and became opponents of the Saddam regime. A third source was printed material published in the West and in Israel, regarding both the various wars and Iraqi activities in the sphere of unconventional weaponry (NBC).

Information in the Arabic language remains the domain of a limited number of Western readers, and a large amount of it has never before been printed in the West. In general, the West “discovered” Iraq only after its invasion of Kuwait in 1990, and everything that occurred before that date in the Saddam era regarding the military remains largely unknown territory. As a result, I found it necessary to devote considerable attention to this unfamiliar period, which formed the basis of subsequent developments.

I was faced with considerable difficulties in obtaining and analyzing information about military matters as they appeared in the Iraqi press at that time. The first problem stemmed from the fact that some of the material did not reach me in real time or for years afterward. The second, even more significant, stemmed from the fact that the Iraqi press, as is customary in such countries, was under state control and obeyed its dictates; thus, it did not always report all issues, even deliberately ignoring some of them. The third, related to processing the material, involved the need to cope with the restrictions imposed by Iraqi censorship, which chose to conceal certain information according to its own interests.

To this must be added the need to cope with the Iraqi custom of calling units by various official names, whether the actual name (generally drawn from Arab and Muslim history, and see Appendix B dealing with heritage) or “fictitious” names (generally ad hoc names of officers), making it difficult to identify various units and their activities in the field. For example, the “Khalid Formation” could refer to a tank regiment by that name, or a brigade that bore that name or whose commanding officer was named Khalid at the time the article or news item was published.

Newspaper articles included descriptions from the battlefield, interviews with commanders and officers, including senior officers, visits of the regime’s senior officials to units and to the front, awards of citations to officers or units that excelled in battle, and details about the activities of the various forces and units, including their histories and successes in various campaigns. The written material was accompanied by dozens of photographs, which revealed details regarding the activities of the units and their fighting, weaponry and equipment, officers, and so on. All of these formed part of a broad propaganda effort aimed at strengthening Saddam’s regime, while ridiculing and condemning Iraq’s chief enemies: Iran, Israel and the United States.

The publication of information about military matters in the Iraqi press over such a long period was an unusual, unprecedented phenomenon compared to the state of the media in other countries in the Arab world, raising questions regarding the Iraqi regime’s motivations for publishing it, as well as its reliability. In my opinion, there were two main reasons for the regime’s attitude toward the media in the course of Saddam’s reign, and especially during the period of the Iranian war. The first was to strengthen the army’s will to fight and the morale of the civilian population, which carried a significant burden of the war effort. The second was the need to demonstrate considerable self-confidence against the enemy, as a form of psychological warfare.

Regarding the degree of reliability of the information appearing in the media, it may be established fairly confidently that, although on the surface it may be suspect of bias and deception, it seems to me that the Iraqis avoided deliberately presenting false information in the press, though it did not always appear close to the events and definitely did not deal with failures. Furthermore, in the 1990s the Iraqis began publishing the memoirs of senior officers in the wars against Iran, Israel, and the Coalition forces, as well as various research studies that were performed retroactively, which uncovered additional information regarding army activities during those periods. I also received corroboration of these data from authentic Iraqi material. This took the form of documents retrieved from Iraq by the United States after the 2003 war, which I had the privilege of studying at the research center housing them, namely the Conflict Records Research Center (CRRC), under the Institute for National Strategic Studies (INSS) at the National Defense University (NDU) in Washington, D.C.

An additional difficulty in writing a study chiefly based on media totally under government control involves the researcher’s ability to examine things and present them objectively, without taking into account the regime’s propaganda input. It was not an easy task to determine the boundary between the facts—which should be presented as objectively as possible in a historical study—and propaganda that loudly acclaims an army, its leadership, and senior command, which were not always deserving of it.

Another problem appeared in the English version with regard to recording Iraqi names. During the translation process I found that it is possible to write the name in more than one option. The Iraqis used to mention the person’s name and also the names of his father and grandfather, but sometimes omitted the family name, or added the place of origin of the man (e.g., Al-Tikriti).

Because I do not have the family names of some of the Iraqis who are mentioned in the book, I preferred to put their names in the index as they appear in the text, and not as the other names that start with the family name.

In my capacity as an intelligence officer, my familiarity with the Iraqi Army began at the end of 1968, when it was active on two separate fronts—against the Kurdish uprising and on the eastern front against Israel; Iraq sent forces to Jordan during the Six-Day War, which remained in northern Jordan until their return to Iraq during the events of “Black September” in 1970. Later I “met up” with this army in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, when a large Iraqi force was sent to the Golan Heights to fight against the IDF.

My next encounter with that army was in 1980 on the eve of the Iran–Iraq War, which particularly interested me and aroused my curiosity. The “secrets” of the Iraqi Army were then revealed in all that army’s dimensions—historical, conceptual, organizational, and operational—including successes and failures and the manner in which it was run by the Iraqi leadership, especially by the figure at its head, Saddam Hussein. At the same time, I was left with many unsolved riddles and questions, some of which were resolved by the material that was later brought out of Iraq, as mentioned above.

With the conclusion of that period in Iraq’s history and the dismantling of the army, which had transformed it into a regional power, in addition to the lack of a comprehensive study about this army, I decided to publish the material that I had accumulated over an extended period and bring it to the public’s attention. I hope that this book will shed additional light on this military power, which decisively influenced events in the Middle East, especially in the last quarter of the twentieth century and the beginning of the twenty-first.

The study presented in this volume includes and encompasses all the components of Iraqi power, the Iraqi Army, including all its branches and corps, as well as the various security- and defense-related forces. As far as possible, a detailed picture is presented of the Iraqi Army during those years, especially during its wars.

The book is divided into five parts:

The first part deals with the historical development of the army and the wars it participated in from its establishment in January 1921 until the beginning of Saddam’s presidency in July 1979.

The second part focuses on the war against Iran (1980–1988).

The third part covers the period from the end of the Iranian war and the invasion of Kuwait until the “Mother of All Battles” War against the Coalition forces and the Intifada that broke out in its wake (1988–1991).

The fourth part centers on the deterioration of the army at the conclusion of the war in Kuwait, the struggle against the United Nations and the Coalition inspection efforts, and the collapse and fall of the regime during the Second Gulf War against the Coalition forces (1991–2003).

The fifth part presents the power components of the Iraqi Army, especially during the reign of Saddam Hussein.

In the course of preparing and actually writing the current study, I was greatly helped by a number of people who enriched the book and improved its contents, all of whom I would like to acknowledge. First of all, my heartfelt thanks go out to my friend Prof. Amatzia Baram, who has been studying the Iraqi scene for many years and is considered an international expert on the subject. Amatzia assisted me in obtaining additional material from his private library and that of Haifa University, which filled in crucial information gaps regarding various fields and topics. His learned comments and insights made a major contribution to my understanding of the matters I deal with and present in this book. In addition, I am grateful for his personal assessment of the volume, as expressed in his introduction (which appears below) and the support he provided in the course of the project.

OEBPS/xhtml/11_Introduction.xhtml:
Introduction to the English Edition

Kevin M. Woods

In Wars of Modern Babylon, Pesach Malovany has created a nearly comprehensive and accessible reference work that covers both the history and the substance of the Iraqi Army. By leveraging a lifetime of professional study, carefully using all available sources, and consulting with some of the top scholars in the field, Pesach has created a masterwork and performed an incredible service to current and future scholars. Reminiscent of David M. Glantz’s comprehensive works on the history of the Red Army, Wars of Modern Babylon will serve as a cornerstone for any serious research on the Iraqi state or its wars.

My involvement with the history of the Iraqi military goes back to a series of studies I led in the aftermath of the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. When the regime fell, the meticulously kept state records of one of the Middle East’s more enduring symbols of authoritarian power were exposed to scrutiny. Government officials, analysts, and scholars all understood the potential of this material. After several false starts, I was part of an effort to make a portion of the captured records available to nongovernment scholars at the Conflict Records Research Center, located at the National Defense University in Washington, D.C.

For longtime students of Iraq, access to these kinds of records was a boon to the scholarship of not only Iraq, but also the wider Middle East and international relations at the end of the twentieth century. For a professional intelligence analyst who spent decades trying to decipher the inner working of Saddam Hussein’s military from scraps of conflicting information, this must have seemed like a dream come true. One of those long-serving professionals was retired Colonel Pesach Malovany, formerly of the Israeli Defense Forces.

I first met Pesach in 2011 while he was finishing the research for the original Hebrew version of this masterwork on the Iraqi military. Pesach and noted Israeli scholar of Iraq Dr. Amatzia Baram were visiting the Center to review recently released records. Unlike many of the scholars I met while visiting the records, Pesach already had an almost encyclopedic knowledge of his subject. Yet here was a fundamentally new source. So despite years of work, to say nothing of a nearly complete manuscript, Pesach quickly dove in. He was a man driven to try to confirm his earlier assessments, resolve long conflicting sources, and find answers to some outstanding mysteries.

My first impression of Pesach was not dissimilar to my encounters with other career intelligence officers—regardless of nationality. I saw an intense, stoic, and politely impatient analyst ready to get on with the business at hand. But in our discussions over several days and subsequent exchanges during the past few years, I came to appreciate one of the things that made Pesach different. As a researcher, Pesach carried into his new passion an intensity born of the real life-or-death responsibility of his earlier studies of the Iraqi Army. He combines the careful judgment and intuition of a career intelligence officer with a historian’s eye for important details and narrative style.

Wars of Modern Babylon seeks to capture the history of an army as that army saw itself. I suppose documenting the who, what, when, and where of an army that served a series of authoritarian regimes is not terribly dissimilar to the work of historians trying to understand the ancient armies of Sumer and Akkad 5,000 years before. Where historians of the ancient Middle East pore over archaeological sites in search of images, names, and scraps of narrative, Pesach has spent decades piecing together the history of an army largely through the modern equivalent of a dig site. His synthesis of news accounts, declassified intelligence reporting, occasional memoirs, and captured records has gone a long way to preserve the history of an army that, given the political and social chaos in Iraq, might otherwise become as unexplored as its ancient predecessors.

Students of Iraq’s modern history already know the central role the army played in shaping events. The scholarship, with some notable exceptions, treats the Iraqi Army as a monolithic actor. The realities, explicated in this volume, are shown to be much more complex. Everything from the demographic mix of leaders at various points in time to the complex and sometimes fleeting honorific titles for critical military formations are meticulously presented within an encyclopedic structure.

It has always been true that victors write—or certainly control—the history of wars, and this is especially true for armies of closed regimes like Iraq. Pesach’s work is an attempt to place the Iraqi Army’s voice back into the historical conversation. While its readers and other scholars must give this voice the weight it deserves, this book provides the essential starting point for any such evaluation. Pesach’s work fills long-standing voids by giving shape and personality to an army that both shaped and reflected one of the most influential states in the modern Middle East.

Introduction

The Iraqi army, 1921–2003: From suppressing internal uprisings and political involvement to the battlefield

The Iraqi Army, whose performance in the field fluctuated between prolonged failure (in 1941, 1967, 1980, and 1982), relative success (in 1973 and 1983–1990), failure (in 1991), and ultimate failure (in 2003), has won an impressive memorial in Pesach Malovany’s profound, monumental study.

The Iraqi Army was established under British auspices on 6 January 1921, approximately seven months before the coronation of Faysal I, founder of the Hashemite monarchy in Baghdad. The founders of the army were former Ottoman officers who had joined the Arab desert rebellion, which aided the British in the First World War against the Ottoman Empire. It was a small, poorly equipped standing army with limited abilities. At the same time, even in its infancy, this army set a path for itself from which it did not waver until its destruction in the spring of 2003.

First, most of the officers serving in the army were and remained members of the Sunni Arab minority; rising through the ranks, this ethnic monopoly became even more pronounced. For example, in 1936 about 70 percent of the highest-ranking officers were Sunnis, and almost all of them were Arabs, although the percentage of Sunni Arabs in the population was a bit less than 20 percent. Similarly, from a random sample it appears that of 60 officers bearing the rank of general (brigadier general and up) in 1986, only 15 or 16 were Shi’ites (25–27 percent), one was a Kurd, two were Turkmens, and the rest were Sunni Arabs.

This represents a significant advance in Shi’ite representation as opposed to most earlier periods, but demonstrates that the broad potential for command to be found in the Shi’ite population (which made up 50–55 percent of the population) did not come to expression, adversely affecting the quality of the military leadership. The overrepresentation of Sunni Arabs among the army command helped preserve Sunni Arab hegemony at the top echelons of power, a phenomenon that characterized all the various regimes—even those that were in bitter opposition to one another—from 1921 to 2003.

Second, under the influence of charismatic ideologues such as Sate’ al-Husri and Sami Shawkat, the Iraqi Army quickly became the flag bearer of nationalist militarism and extreme pan-Arabism. The military leadership ridiculed civilian politicians for being spineless and compromising, at times even accusing them of treason. Starting from 1936, the military leadership became deeply involved in politics, and from that time on they also instigated a number of military coups.

Apart from the coup led by General Bakr Sidki (1936–1937) and the rule of General Qasim (1958–1963), all the other military coups and the periods of their rule were imbued with deep pan-Arab ideology. Only the Ba’ath regime (1968–2003) put an end to this involvement. This government cultivated the army more than ever before, but prevented it from influencing policy. It even turned the tables: from the early 1970s onward, the party infiltrated all ranks of the army and imposed its ideas on the officers. Complete control of the army leadership made it possible for the Ba’ath regime to adopt a very pragmatic policy, which delayed pan-Arab commitments to the distant future and emphasized the need first and foremost to serve the interests of the regime. Thus, for example, when the political leadership decided not to come to the aid of the Palestinian organizations in their struggle against King Hussein during the events of “Black September,” the army acted according to the dictates of the political leadership, and did not dare oppose them. In addition, when Saddam decided to invade Iran—and later Kuwait—instead of sending his divisions to fight against Israel, the military leadership accepted his decision.

This obedience was achieved by what was called in Iraq “terror and temptation” (al-tarhib wal-targhib). An officer who refused an order, insulted the president, or took an unacceptable position was relieved of his duties, imprisoned, or even executed, and his family was made to pay the price. On the other hand, with the expansion of the army, many officers enjoyed rapid promotion, while their pay and social benefits were greatly improved. At the same time, it seems that the Iraqi Army’s leadership remained pan-Arab and militarist until its final days. In its own eyes it represented the values and interests of Iraq and the Arabs better than any other official body.

Third, the Iraqi Army demonstrated brutal efficiency on most of the occasions when it was sent to suppress internal uprisings, but failed in almost every clash with other armies until 1982, and in all of them after 1990. In 1933 it suppressed an Assyrian uprising and butchered the civilian population. In 1935–1936 it brutally suppressed an uprising of Shi’ite tribes. The Iraqi Army was defeated in its struggle against the Kurdish rebellion as long as the Kurds received outside help, but in 1975 it succeeded in quashing that rebellion. In 1991 the Iraqi Army successfully and brutally suppressed an extensive Shi’ite uprising, and in 1988 and again in 1991 it ground the Kurdish rebels to dust, partially with the use (in 1988) of chemical weapons.

The army’s successes against foreign armies—the major reason for an army’s existence—were far less impressive. Nevertheless, since, due to tribal and ethnic divisions and the rivalry between warring factions, the Iraqi nation had no other symbol of unity and national pride, the army became the chief symbol of Iraqi nationalism. Apart from the Kurdish minority (about 18 percent of the population), most Iraqis viewed the army favorably, while ignoring the regime being served by that army. Even many of those who witnessed the bloody suppression of the 1991 uprising did not hold the army responsible, but rather pointed an accusing finger at Saddam and his regime.

Fourth, especially during the Ba’ath regime, but to a large extent also under earlier regimes, the rulers in every era had to weigh up what was more important to them: the army’s loyalty or the quality of its leadership. In the long run, they all made the same decision. On the one hand, they needed the army in order to withstand powerful external enemies (including Iran, Turkey, and even Saudi Arabia), but on the other hand, it hung like the Sword of Damocles over their heads. Thus, in every case where politicians had doubts about a particular officer’s loyalty, they chose to discharge him, even if he had proved himself on the battlefield. This policy was intensified by the Ba’ath regime after 1968, and reached its peak in the course of Saddam Hussein’s presidency (1979–2003), thus greatly damaging the performance of the Iraqi Army in its encounters with foreign armies.

Pesach Malovany spreads before the reader a broader panorama of the Iraqi Army than any that has been displayed before. Relying mainly on Iraqi sources passed through the filter of his professional criticism, in addition to a variety of other sources, Malovany has created a huge tapestry. Thousands of reports, interviews, news photos, and personal accounts of battles all combine together to illuminate 80 years of an army that was and is no more.

In 1941 the Iraqi Army encountered a foreign army for the first time when it engaged in battle with units of the British Army. It was easily defeated by a much smaller force. In 1948 in the Palestinian War and in 1967 in the Six-Day War, the Iraqi Army failed in most of its missions. In 1973 the army had relative success during the Yom Kippur War. Its forces demonstrated a fighting spirit, despite the heavy losses they incurred.

Malovany explains Iraq’s unimpressive performance against the IDF by objective factors: the Iraqis were not informed by their Syrian and Egyptian brothers of their intention to start a war. The Iraqi units were lacking in tank transporters/carriers, which arrived at the front bit by bit. In addition, they acted without effective coordination with their Syrian hosts. However, the Iraqi armored brigade that did arrive on time immediately engaged with the Israeli division commanded by Maj. Gen. Dan Laner. The latter was caught unawares, being short of ammunition and petrol, while its soldiers were exhausted from constant hard fighting. The Iraqi force succeeded in blocking Laner’s advance toward the outskirts of Damascus. In fact, Israel had no intention of conquering the Syrian capital, but only of assuming convenient artillery positions. In any event, the Iraqis were quite justified in future political debates with Hafez al-Assad’s regime when they claimed that it was they who had saved Damascus.

This partial success disappeared without a trace at the beginning of the Iraq-Iran War (1980–1988). Malovany presents the Iraqi Army in all its weakness during the first two years of that war: despite its obvious advantage regarding both the quantity and quality of weapons and numbers of regular units, the army failed in its mission to conquer Khuzestan Province, eventually even relinquishing the territorial gains it had made. Yet surprisingly enough, Malovany reveals the impressive improvement that took place in the Iraqi Army’s performance from 1983 until the end of the war.

Whereas the world had received the impression of static trench warfare resembling the European front in the First World War, Malovany presents the reader with a detailed picture of a war of movement. It is true that the lines changed only slightly, but not due to stasis. The Iranians staged massive attacks, initiatives involving thousands of soldiers and at very close range, at times involving bayonets and grenades, and on each occasion at a different point on a front stretching 1,200 km. In most cases, they did manage to take control of considerable Iraqi territories. However, this was always followed by an Iraqi counterattack relying mainly on rapid movement of armored forces supported by massive artillery fire, and at times with army aviation (helicopters) and air force plane cover, and with the participation of well-trained infantry forces. Here Malovany refutes an additional myth according to which air–ground support was clumsy and ineffective due to Saddam’s fear that his planes would be used against him.

Supplied with useful information from American satellites, Iraqi intelligence almost always identified Iranian plans of attack in good time, thus managing to concentrate reserve forces behind the front lines ready for counterattack. Apart from the Iranian forces’ conquest of the Al-Faw Peninsula (in February 1986), the Iraqis always reoccupied any Iraqi territory taken over by the Iranians. The occupation of Al-Faw may thus be seen as an exception that proved the rule.

In the spring of 1988, the Iraqis opened an offensive that ended only in the summer, when Khomeini agreed to a ceasefire as a result of his realization that the Iraqi forces had totally decimated the Iranian forces in Khuzestan. This was a huge victory for Iraq, which led the Iraqi generals to demand of Saddam to continue fighting with the aim of conquering the entire area, but Saddam refused. He seems to have finally realized the limits of his military power, and was not interested in motivating Khomeini and the Iranian nation to embark on a holy war. Malovany’s description of the Iraq-Iran War is more three-dimensional and comprehensive than anything published up to now.

Another swing of the pendulum occurred in 1991. The Kuwaiti invasion, upon which Malovany sheds new light, was quick, efficient, and uncomplicated. Conversely, when describing the 1991 conflict (and later that of 2003) based on accounts of senior Iraqi officers and American experts, in addition to his own analytical experience, Malovany uncovers Iraq in all its weakness.

The first and most important conclusion the reader arrives at is that Iraq’s biggest mistake was political and strategic: it was out of the question for Iraq to enter into military conflict with the greatest army in the world. No nation, especially a Third World country, even though it possessed a huge army with considerable fighting experience against other Third World countries, was capable of victory over the United States Army. Even the IDF, with all its experience and capabilities, made every effort to avoid a direct clash with a world power (the Soviet Union) during the War of Attrition. However, apart from this serious misjudgment, Malovany enumerates other blunders that prevented the Iraqi force from exacting a much higher price.

It was already clear in 2003 that the Iraqi army couldn’t compete with the U.S. Army, but senior Iraqi officers were afraid to inform Saddam of this fact. As in 1991, the Iraqi president, an incurable optimist, believed that the Americans would not attack. Furthermore, he believed (again as in 1991) that even if they did attack, his army would be capable of delaying their advance and causing them heavy losses until they stopped in their tracks and the international community came to Iraq’s aid. Again, as in 1991, his officers were afraid of revealing the truth about the unbridgeable gap between the two armies. Malovany indicates that it was enough for one general to warn Saddam in 1990 and be discharged to silence all of his comrades in 2003; it appears that they feared Saddam more than they feared the Americans.

The result is well known. The reign of terror imposed by Saddam upon his officers resulted in a second defeat, and this time a decisive death blow, which Saddam paid for with his life. However, Malovany is not satisfied with this explanation, but enumerates all the tactical and strategic errors made by the Iraqis up until their final battle, preventing them from delaying the Americans and maybe even causing distress to the unpopular Bush administration (considering that in the United States there was strong opposition to the war). Apparently, Saddam himself was directly responsible for a large number of these errors. He refused to face reality even when he should have been arranging an escape route for himself, his family, and his senior ministers. His army, including its elite units, crashed around him before he realized what was happening. How did this come about? The reader will discover the answer in Pesach Malovany’s dramatic account.

Professor Emeritus Dr. Amatzia Baram
Department of the History of the Middle East
and Director of the Center for Iraq Studies
University of Haifa, Israel
